pages.text: ReCG — Worked Example ReCG · PVLDB 2024 · Worked Example Discovering a JSON schema from the leaves up ReCG infers a set of JSON schemas from documents alone. It resolves instance trees bottom-up, clusters the partially derived objects at each level, generalizes the clusters into a spectrum of candidate schema sets, and lets the minimum description length principle pick the winner inside a beam search. Step through one small collection below. { } Given three JSON documents and no schema, which set of JSON schemas should describe the collection — specific enough to reject junk, general enough to accept the documents we have not seen yet? OUTPUT Z = {S₁, S₂} ◀ Prev 1 / 10 Next ▶ Problem JSON schema discovery: from documents alone, derive a schema set that is neither one-schema-per-document nor accept-anything. Idea Existing algorithms derive schemas top-down and must classify a node before its children are known. ReCG goes bottom-up: children first, so each decision is informed. Stage 1 The lowest level is resolved first: every primitive value becomes a primitive schema node. Arrays would be handled here too (generalized to a single ∗ edge, then clustered once). Stage 2 · cluster At level 2 the three info objects are CD-instances. They are clustered by a Jaccard-style distance over (key, child-schema) pairs: {c₁, c₃} together, c₂ apart. Stage 2 · generalize From the clusters ReCG does not pick one schema set — it enumerates a spectrum, from the initial clusters to repeatedly merged (more general) ones. Each is a sibling state of stage 2. MDL States compete on minimum description length : bits to write the schemas plus bits to write the data given the schemas. The balanced state wins. Stage 3 At the roots the same cluster → generalize → cost loop runs once more. Here the two-schema set beats the merged one: merging would admit key combinations nobody has seen. Search The whole run is a beam search over states: each stage clusters, generalizes into siblings, scores them with MDL and keeps the best three. Output The result is an ordinary JSON Schema set: two document types sharing one info definition with an optional key. ✦ Why it works Informed decisions (bottom-up), a spectrum of candidates (cluster-and-generalize) and a principled judge (MDL) — each fixes one failure of top-down discovery. pages.text: LILaC — Worked Example LILaC · EMNLP 2025 · Worked Example How a question about a photo two hops away gets answered LILaC retrieves from documents that mix paragraphs, tables and images. It builds a two-layer component graph offline, decomposes the query into modality-specific subqueries online, and walks the graph edge by edge, scoring each edge with late interaction over fine-grained subcomponents. Step through one query below. ❓ In the mausoleum built by the Mughal emperor who married Mumtaz Mahal , how many slender minarets surround the central dome? ANSWER Four ◀ Prev 1 / 10 Next ▶ Setup Three Wikipedia-style documents, each a sequence of paragraph / image / table components; one paragraph hyperlinks to the other two pages. Offline · 1 Every component becomes a two-level component tree : sentences under a paragraph, header+row segments under a table, detected objects under an image. Offline · 2 Coarse nodes are linked by a clique inside each document and by hyperlink edges across documents; then every node is embedded once. Online · 1 The query is decomposed by an LLM into three subqueries, each classified into a modality that becomes the embedding instruction. Online · 2 Seed: the top-b (b = 2) coarse nodes by similarity to the whole query — one nearest-neighbour search over V₀, nothing else. Online · 3 From the seeds, every incident edge is a candidate; each edge gets a relevance score computed now , from fine-grained nodes — no edge embeddings exist. Online · 4 Edge-level late interaction : an edge is scored by matching each subquery against the subcomponents hanging off both endpoints, then summing the per-subquery maxima. (Similarities here are illustrative.) Online · 5 Beam search over edges: keep the b best edges, make their endpoints the new candidates, repeat for n i iterations. The search never scores more than a few dozen edges. Result The final subgraph's nodes are returned as a ranked list; the multimodal LLM answers from the Taj Mahal photo. ✦ Why it works Granularity, structure and modality are handled by three separate mechanisms — and the expensive one (the LLM) runs once per query, not per hop.
